edge.title: The gold with a story attached
edge.setup: A stranger or a friend-of-a-friend has gold — inherited, found, blessed, or 'from a closed jeweller'. He will sell it well below market, or hand you a little as proof and offer more if you put money in. The story is detailed and slightly sacred, and there is a reason it must stay quiet.
edge.tell: A price below market, with a story that explains why it must be quick and secret.
move: Never pay, lend or hand over anything before the metal is tested. A small sample being real is the bait, not the proof.
Test at a BIS-hallmarked jeweller or an assay centre of your choosing, not one the seller suggests.
Buy gold only from a registered jeweller who gives a bill and hallmarked pieces. If a seller refuses a bill, that refusal is the answer.
If you have already paid, report on 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in, and to the local police, the same day.
edge.why: A genuine bargain does not need a secret, a sacred reason or a deadline. The story exists to make you skip the one step that kills the con, which is verification. The secrecy also stops you from asking someone who would say no.
edge.variants: Same shape: 'treasure' found while digging, double-your-money schemes, a tout selling 'seized' goods cheap, crypto 'insider tips'.
edge.anchor: Bengaluru police reports describe a goldsmith duped of ₹1.3 crore after a man claimed a goddess had given him 5 kg of gold (Times of India).

lens.name: Asymmetric information
lens.one_line: When one side knows much more than the other, the market degrades toward the worse goods.
lens.detail: If buyers can't tell good used cars from bad, they offer an average price. Owners of genuinely good cars refuse to sell at that price and leave the market, so the average quality drops, so the price drops further. Quality collapses — not from dishonesty, but from unverifiability. Every real fix is a verification mechanism: warranties, certification, inspection, reputation.
elsewhere: Freelance marketplaces race to the bottom without reviews.
Insurance pools get sicker when only the sick buy in.
A degree works partly as a costly signal of something an employer can't directly see.
lens.test: What can the other side see that I can't — and what would make it visible?
lens.today: An AI survey of North Bengaluru's roads has flagged over 14,000 potholes, about one every 173 metres, and a pothole app is reported to identify the contractor for each road. Until now, the state of a road was something the contractor knew and you could only suffer; a public map makes it checkable. Verification, not goodwill, is what changes behaviour.

moved.so_what: Do not stand near a fuel pump during a crash or fire; move well upwind and call 112. Keep a few metres' distance from ring main units and transformers on the street.
